a: I laid all this on my heart
p: Qohelet's usual phrase for thinking something through. The rare verb that follows means to sift or test.
b: Natan el-libbi, "I gave to my heart", is Qohelet's way of saying he set his mind to a task (1:13, 17; 8:9, 16). For the ancient Hebrew reader the heart was the seat of thinking and choosing more than of feeling. The next verb, lavur, "to make clear", comes from a root meaning to sift or purify (compare 3:18, "God is testing them"), and it appears nowhere else in this form. The Greek and the Syriac seem to have read slightly different letters here, "and my heart saw all this" (see the variant). Either way, chapter 9 opens as a report on a long inquiry, not a passing mood.

a: are in God's hand
t: In God's hand: safe, or simply held?
p: The hand of God can mean his care or simply his control. Qohelet seems to mean that people cannot steer their own lives.
b: "God" here, as everywhere in the book, is ha'elohim, "the God", with the article; Ecclesiastes never uses the divine name YHWH ("the LORD"). To be "in someone's hand" in Hebrew means to be in his power (Genesis 16:6; Proverbs 21:1). Many readers hear comfort: the righteous are kept by God, as in Wisdom of Solomon 3:1, which may echo this verse. But Qohelet's next words cut against an easy comfort: no one can tell whether what lies ahead is love or hate. Most commentators (Fox, Seow, Krüger) take the point to be control rather than protection. The righteous and the wise do not hold their own future; God does, and he does not show his hand. The Targum turns it toward reward: the deeds of the righteous are stored up before God.

a: Love, or hate: a human being knows neither.
p: The Hebrew does not say whose love or hate is meant: God's favor, other people's feelings, or a person's own.
b: The line is compressed: "both love and hate, the human does not know; everything is before them." Three readings are offered. (1) No one can know whether God loves or hates him, judging by what happens to him (Rashi, Ibn Ezra, Fox). (2) No one knows whether love or hatred from others lies ahead (Seow, Longman). (3) People do not even know what they themselves will come to love or hate. The first fits the next verse best: since one fate comes to everyone, good fortune is no proof of God's favor and disaster no proof of his anger. Job's friends had argued the opposite (Job 4:7–8).
orig: גַּם־אַהֲבָה גַם־שִׂנְאָה אֵין יוֹדֵעַ הָאָדָם (gam-ahavah gam-sin'ah 'en yodea' ha'adam)

a: One fate comes to the righteous and to the wicked
p: Qohelet lists five pairs, moral and religious, and says death treats both sides the same.
b: Miqreh, "fate", is what finally happens to someone, above all death (see 2:14; 3:19). The list moves from moral words (righteous and wicked, good) to the language of worship (clean and unclean, the one who sacrifices and the one who does not) and then to oaths. The last pair is a puzzle: is the one who "swears" the careless one, and the one "afraid of an oath" the careful one (compare 5:4–6; 8:2)? Most think so, which means the pattern flips: in the last pair the bad comes first. Some think the reversal is deliberate, to show that the order does not matter. In 9:2 the Hebrew has "the good" with no partner; the Greek and Syriac add "and the bad" (see the variant).

a: madness fills their hearts all their lives
p: Holelot, 'madness', is Qohelet's word for the senseless behavior he studied alongside wisdom (1:17; 2:12).
b: Qohelet set out "to learn what madness and folly are" (1:17), and here he gives the verdict on human nature: the heart is "full of evil", and holelot, wild senselessness, fills it as long as people live. He is not describing a mental illness but the reckless way people act, perhaps made worse by knowing that death is coming anyway (compare 8:11). The verse sits close to the Bible's other blunt statements about the human heart (Genesis 6:5; Genesis 8:21; Jeremiah 17:9). It also explains 9:7–10: if this is the human condition, the gifts of bread, wine and love are all the more to be taken as gifts.

a: Then it is off to the dead.
p: The Hebrew ends abruptly, 'and after it, to the dead', without a verb, as if Qohelet breaks off.
b: The Hebrew is ve'acharav el-hammetim: "and after it (or 'after him'), to the dead." There is no verb. English versions supply one ("they go", "they join"), but the bluntness is part of the effect: a whole life of evil and madness, and then, simply, the dead. "After it" may mean after their life, or after the madness; "after him" would point to each person's own end. The Plain keeps the clipped feel with "Then it is off to the dead."

a: has something to trust in
p: Bittachon, 'trust' or 'confidence', appears elsewhere only in the Assyrian officer's taunt to Hezekiah.
b: Most versions say the living have "hope". The Hebrew bittachon is closer to "something to rely on". It is rare: the only other uses are the Assyrian officer's question, "What is this trust of yours that you trust in?" (2 Kings 18:19; Isaiah 36:4), where the same noun is rendered "trust". Qohelet's point is modest. He does not promise the living a good outcome; he says only that while you are alive something can still happen, and once you are dead nothing can. The next verse shows how thin the advantage is: the living at least know that they will die.

a: It is better to be a living dog than a dead lion.
t: A living dog and a dead lion
p: In Israel the dog was a scavenger and an insult, the lion a symbol of royal strength. Even so, alive beats dead.
b: Dogs in the ancient Near East were mostly half-wild scavengers, and "dog" or "dead dog" was a stock insult (1 Samuel 17:43; 2 Samuel 9:8; 2 Kings 8:13). The lion was the king of beasts and a symbol of Judah and its kings (Genesis 49:9; Proverbs 30:30). So the saying turns the scale of honor upside down: the lowest living thing beats the noblest dead one. The rabbis noticed that it seems to clash with 4:2, where Qohelet praises the dead above the living. Bavli Shabbat 30a raises the clash, beside Psalm 115:17, in a question put to Rav Tanhum of Nevi ("Solomon, where is your wisdom?"), and resolves it by applying the verses to different people. When the sages' wish to withdraw the book comes up on the next page (Shabbat 30b), the contradictions cited are other ones: 7:3 and 8:15, each set against 2:2.
r: 1 Samuel 17:43; 2 Samuel 9:8; 2 Kings 8:13; Genesis 49:9; Proverbs 30:30; 4:2; Psalm 115:17; 2:2; 7:3; 8:15

a: the dead do not know a thing
t: "The dead know nothing": what does Qohelet claim?
p: One of the Bible's most quoted lines about death. Readers disagree on whether it describes the dead as such or only life under the sun.
b: Read in its setting, the line means that the dead have no share in life "under the sun": no knowledge of it, no wages, no memory, no love or hate (9:5–6, 10). Most scholars think Qohelet shared the older Israelite picture of Sheol as a place of silence and shadow (Psalm 6:5; Psalm 88:10–12; Psalm 115:17; Job 14:21), and that he did not know or did not accept the hope of resurrection found in Daniel 12:2. The rabbis read the verse morally: the "living" are the righteous, who are called living even in death, and the "dead" are the wicked, who are called dead even in life (Bavli Berakhot 18a–b). Seventh-day Adventists and Jehovah's Witnesses take it as a plain teaching that the dead are unconscious until the resurrection. Catholic, Orthodox and most Protestant teachers read it as speaking of the dead's relation to this world, within the Old Testament's partial view, and not as denying a conscious life with God. See the card on this chapter.

a: There are no more wages for them
p: Sakhar, 'wages', and zikhram, 'their memory', sound alike in Hebrew. The dead lose both.
b: Sakhar is a worker's pay (Genesis 30:28; Deuteronomy 24:15), and so a reward. Qohelet pairs it with zikhram, "the memory of them", which has the same last two consonants in the same order (ś-k-r and z-k-r); only the first letter differs. The dead get no more pay and no more remembrance: no gain from their toil and no lasting name. That links back to his opening complaint that "there is no memory" of earlier generations (1:11; 2:16). Later Jewish and Christian readers, who believed in reward after death, heard "no more wages" as "no more chance to earn" (so the Targum: once dead, a person can no longer gain merit).

a: And they have no share any longer, forever
p: Cheleq, 'share', is a person's allotted portion in life. The dead have lost theirs forever, 'under the sun'.
b: Cheleq is the share a person is given: a plot of land, a cut of booty, and in Qohelet the portion of enjoyment God gives with life and work (2:10; 3:22; 5:18–19). In 9:9 the living are told to take their share. Here the dead have none, "forever" (le'olam). The phrase that closes the verse limits the claim: no share "in anything that is done under the sun." Readers who believe in a life to come stress that limit (so Jerome and the Targum, which adds "in this world"). Readers who see Qohelet as denying any afterlife stress "forever". Both agree that for life on earth the loss is total.

a: Come, eat your bread in joy
p: In the Old Babylonian Gilgamesh, the alewife Siduri gives advice strikingly close to 9:7–9. What does the parallel show?
b: In the Old Babylonian version of the Epic of Gilgamesh (about 1800 BC), Gilgamesh, wandering in search of eternal life, meets Siduri, who keeps a tavern at the edge of the world. She tells him he will not find the life he seeks, because the gods kept life for themselves. So, she says, fill your belly, make merry day and night, wear clean clothes, wash your head, delight in the child who holds your hand, and let your wife enjoy your embrace. The order is close to 9:7–9: food and joy, clean clothes, the head, a wife. The speech is missing from the later Standard Babylonian epic, so if Qohelet knew it, he knew an older form, or a saying that had travelled on its own. Van der Toorn argues for real knowledge; others see a shared tradition, like the Egyptian harpers' songs. Either way, Qohelet changes one thing: he grounds the advice in God, who "has already" accepted it (9:7).

a: with a good heart drink your wine
p: Qohelet echoes the Psalms' praise of wine as God's gift, not a call to drunkenness.
b: A "good heart" is a cheerful one (1 Kings 8:66; Esther 1:10, where it is the effect of wine). Psalm 104 praises God for "wine that makes people glad at heart" (Psalm 104:15), and Judges 9:13 has wine that "cheers gods and humans". Qohelet's command is about receiving ordinary gifts with joy, bread and wine being the staples of every meal. Elsewhere the Bible warns sharply against drunkenness (Proverbs 20:1; Proverbs 23:29–35), and Qohelet himself praises princes who eat "to be strong and not to be drunk" (10:17). On the church debates about alcohol, see the cards at Proverbs 20:1 and 23:31.

a: for what you do has already pleased God
p: Does God approve of your deeds, or has he already decided that you may enjoy life? The word 'already' carries the weight.
b: The Hebrew says God kevar ratsah, "has already been pleased with", your ma'asim, "what you do". Most modern scholars take it as a statement about gift: enjoying bread and wine is what God wants, so it needs no further permission (compare 2:24–26; 3:13; 5:19). The Targum reads it of merit: God says to the righteous in the world to come, eat with joy the reward for the bread you gave the poor, because your good deeds have been accepted. Luther read it as a word of grace: a person who trusts God may enjoy daily life with a good conscience, without monkish anxiety. The difference matters for the whole book: is joy a reward, a gift, or a way of making the best of a hard world?
orig: כִּי כְבָר רָצָה הָאֱלֹהִים אֶת־מַעֲשֶׂיךָ (ki khevar ratsah ha'elohim et-ma'asekha)

a: Let your clothes be white all the time
p: White clothes and oil on the head were signs of a festival. The rabbis heard a call to be ready for death.
b: Clean white garments were worn at feasts and on joyful occasions (Esther 8:15), and oil on the head belonged to celebration and welcome (Psalm 23:5; Psalm 45:7; Luke 7:46), while mourners did without it (2 Samuel 14:2). Qohelet means: let every day be a festival. The Egyptian harpers' songs give the same advice: perfume your head and dress in fine linen. The rabbis heard more. Rabbi Eliezer taught, repent one day before your death; since no one knows that day, repent every day, and he cited this verse. Rabbi Yochanan ben Zakkai added a parable: a king invited his servants to a banquet without naming the hour; the wise dressed at once, while the foolish went on working and came in dirty (Bavli Shabbat 153a). The parable is close to Jesus' stories of the wedding garment and the waiting bridesmaids (Matthew 22:11–13; Matthew 25:1–13). Revelation, too, dresses the faithful in white (Revelation 3:4).
r: Esther 8:15; Psalm 23:5; Psalm 45:7; 2 Samuel 14:2; Matthew 22:11–13; Matthew 25:1–13; Revelation 3:4–5

a: See life with a woman you love
p: To 'see' life in Hebrew is to experience and enjoy it, as in Qohelet's refrain 'see good in his toil'.
b: Re'eh chayyim is literally "see life". The verb "see" often means to experience, good or bad: to "see good" is to enjoy (2:1, 24; 3:13; 5:18), and to "see death" is to die (Psalm 89:48). The Plain keeps "See life" so that the reader hears the link with the refrain. The woman has no article in Hebrew: "a woman whom you love", which many take as "your wife" (Proverbs 5:18 has "the woman you married when you were young"). Coming after the harsh lines on women in 7:26–28, this verse is often cited by those who read Qohelet as a lover of ordinary life, and it agrees with Proverbs 18:22: "The one who finds a wife has found something good."

a: all the days of your vapor of a life
p: Hevel is breath, vapor or smoke: real but passing and impossible to grasp. Older English says 'vanity'.
b: Hevel first means breath, mist, vapor or smoke, the puff you see on a cold morning (Psalm 39:5, "nothing but a puff of air"), something a breeze carries off (Isaiah 57:13) or a passing shadow (Psalm 144:4). Qohelet uses it 38 times. The Greek translated it mataiotes and the Latin vanitas, which gave the English "vanity", in the old sense of "emptiness". Modern versions offer "meaningless", "futile", "fleeting" or "enigma", and Fox argues for "absurd": what makes no sense. Each picks one side of the image. Here, in "your vapor of a life", the sense of fleeting is plain; elsewhere it is the sense of unfairness or of what cannot be grasped. The site keeps "vapor" everywhere so that readers can see the same word and decide what it means in each place, as Qohelet's first hearers did.
orig: חַיֵּי הֶבְלֶךָ (chayye hevlekha), "the life of your vapor"

a: Whatever is in your power to do
p: The Hebrew idiom 'what your hand finds' means 'whatever you are able to do'. The verse is often quoted as a motto for hard work.
b: The Hebrew is "all that your hand finds to do", an idiom for what lies within your power or comes your way (1 Samuel 10:7; 1 Samuel 25:8; Judges 9:33). The familiar older wording has made the verse a motto for doing one's job wholeheartedly, often paired with Colossians 3:23. That is not wrong, but the reason Qohelet gives is not that work is noble. It is that Sheol is coming, where nothing can be done. So the verse is closer to "use your strength while you have it", and it belongs with the call to enjoy food, clothes and love in 9:7–9. Jesus says something similar about urgency: "The night is on its way, when nobody can work" (John 9:4).
orig: כֹּל אֲשֶׁר תִּמְצָא יָדְךָ לַעֲשׂוֹת (kol asher timtsa yadekha la'asot)

a: no reckoning
p: Cheshbon is an account or reckoning: the figuring-out Qohelet himself was doing (7:25, 27).
b: Cheshbon is a reckoning, a totting up of results. Qohelet uses it of his own search, when he set out to find wisdom and a reckoning and added one thing to another to reach it (7:25, 27). The Plain renders it "reckoning" in all three places. So the four things that end at death are the very things he spent his life on: doing, reckoning, knowing and being wise. The list has a sharp edge for a sage. All the wisdom he has gathered will stop at the door of Sheol.

a: in Sheol, the place where you are going
p: Sheol is the common grave of all, not a place for the wicked only. Qohelet says 'you' are going there.
b: Sheol is the Hebrew Bible's name for the world of the dead, under the earth, where good and bad alike go down (Genesis 37:35; Psalm 89:48). Qohelet names it only here. He addresses the reader directly, "where you are going", making it personal. The older English "the grave" (KJV) is not wrong but loses the sense of a place. Later Jewish and Christian writings divided the dead in Sheol or Hades into the righteous and the wicked (1 Enoch 22; Luke 16:22–26), but Qohelet does not. For how the churches read 9:5 and 9:10, see the card on this chapter.
r: Genesis 37:35; Psalm 89:48; Psalm 6:5; Isaiah 38:18; 1 Enoch 22; Luke 16:22–26; 3:20; 9:5

a: the race does not belong to the swift
p: Five gifts that should bring their reward do not. Amos and Paul use similar pictures.
b: Speed, strength, wisdom, discernment and knowledge should each bring their prize: the race, the battle, bread, wealth, favor. Qohelet says they do not reliably do so. Amos has the same pictures for the day of judgment, when flight will fail the swift and the warrior will not save himself (Amos 2:14–15). David tells Goliath: "The battle belongs to the LORD" (1 Samuel 17:47). Paul writes that God's mercy does not depend on "the one who runs" (Romans 9:16). Qohelet's point is not God's choice, though, but the gap between gifts and outcome. The line is often quoted as a comfort to the underdog, though in context it is a warning to the gifted.

a: time and chance
p: Pega' is an occurrence, often a mishap. 'Time and chance' may mean 'an unlucky time'.
b: Pega', from a verb meaning to meet or strike, is something that happens to you: Solomon says "There is no adversary, and nothing bad is happening", using the same word for the second phrase (1 Kings 5:4). Paired with 'et, "time", it may be a single idea, "a time of mishap", which suits 9:12's "evil time". Qohelet does not mean a force called Luck or Fate, as the Greeks worshiped Tyche. He means that events strike people without regard to their merits. Jewish and Christian readers have generally held that what looks like chance under the sun is still under God's rule (Proverbs 16:33), and some see Qohelet saying exactly that in 3:1–15, where every "time" belongs to God.

a: do not even know their time
p: 'His time' probably means the time of death or disaster, as in 7:17 and Job 22:16.
b: 'Itto, "his time", is set beside "an evil time" that drops suddenly. In 7:17 Qohelet asks why anyone should die "when it is not your time", and Job speaks of the wicked who "were seized when it was not yet their time" (Job 22:16). So most readers take it as the hour of death or of sudden ruin. The pictures are a hunter's: the fish in a net, the bird in a trap (Proverbs 7:23; Amos 3:5; Habakkuk 1:14–15). Jesus uses the same image for the last day, which will come "like a trap" on those not ready (Luke 21:34–35).

a: siege works
p: The Hebrew word here is the same as 'net' in 9:12. Most read it as siege works; the echo may be deliberate.
b: The Hebrew is metsodim, which elsewhere means nets or snares and is spelled almost exactly like "net" (metsodah) in 9:12. Since a king does not build nets, most scholars read it as metsurim, siege works or ramps (Deuteronomy 20:20), assuming a scribe confused two similar letters, or that the word could mean a siegework in late Hebrew. The ancient versions translate "palisades" or "siege works". The same plural, metsodim, is the "net" of 7:26, the woman "whose heart is a net". Some see a deliberate echo running through the book: the man caught by the trapping woman, the fish and birds caught in 9:12, and now a town caught by a king.

a: There was a small town with few men inside.
t: A true story or a parable?
p: Scholars have looked for a real siege behind the story. Most now read it as a parable about wisdom that is ignored.
b: Readers have tried to name the town. The wise woman of Abel Beth-maacah, who saved her town from Joab (2 Samuel 20:14–22), is the closest biblical story. Others thought of Archimedes, whose machines held off the Romans at Syracuse until it fell in 212 BC, or of sieges in the Persian and Hellenistic wars. None fits closely, and the story has the bare outline of a parable: a small town, a great king, a poor wise man. The rabbis read it as an allegory of the soul: the small town is the body, its few men the limbs, the great king the evil impulse, and the poor wise man the good impulse, which is ignored once the danger passes (Bavli Nedarim 32b). Christian allegorists saw in the poor wise man a picture of Christ, who saved by wisdom and was despised.

a: by his wisdom he rescued the town
t: Did he save it, or could he have?
p: The Hebrew verb can also mean 'he could have rescued it'. Then no one even thought to ask him.
b: The Hebrew umillat normally means "and he rescued". But Hebrew verbs of this form can sometimes express what could have happened, and Fox, among others, reads: "he could have saved the city by his wisdom, but no one thought of that poor man." On that reading the town fell, or was saved some other way, because no one consulted him. That fits 9:16 well: the poor man's wisdom "is looked down on, and no one listens to his words." On the usual reading the town was saved, and then the man was forgotten, which fits the theme of forgotten memory in 1:11; 2:16 and 9:5. Either way the point is that wisdom does not bring its due reward.

a: But a poor man's wisdom is looked down on
p: Ben Sira puts the same observation in sharper form: when a rich man speaks, all are silent; when a poor man speaks, they ask who he is.
b: Qohelet tests his own proverb, "Wisdom is better than might", against what he saw, and finds a limit: wisdom works, but people ignore it when it comes from the poor. Sirach 13:22–23 makes the same point: when the rich man stumbles, many help him, and his foolish talk is praised; when the poor man speaks sense, he gets no hearing. Proverbs had praised the wise man who can take a city (Proverbs 21:22). Qohelet adds that even then, no one remembers him. Paul's words about God choosing what the world counts foolish turn the same observation into a statement of faith (1 Corinthians 1:27).

a: spoken calmly
p: Benachat can mean the words are spoken quietly or heard in a quiet setting. Either way, calm beats shouting.
b: Benachat, "in quietness" or "in calm", may describe how the wise speak (gently, without shouting) or how they are heard (in a calm setting, by those who listen). The Hebrew allows both, and they amount to the same lesson. The contrast is with the za'aqah, the shouted cry, of "a ruler among fools", a ruler who either rules fools or is a fool among them. Isaiah gives the same counsel: "in calm and in trust your strength will lie" (Isaiah 30:15). Proverbs often praises the soft word (Proverbs 15:1; Proverbs 25:15).

a: one sinner can wreck a great deal of good
p: Chote' usually means 'sinner', but the root means 'miss the mark'. The verse leads into 10:1, where a little folly spoils much.
b: The root chata' means to miss a target (Judges 20:16, of slingers who "do not miss"), and so to sin. Here chote' 'echad may be a person, "one sinner", or one error. Some scholars read chet' 'echad, "one sin". The next verse, 10:1, supports the idea: as dead flies spoil perfume, so a little folly outweighs wisdom. Readers have thought of Achan, whose single theft brought defeat on all Israel (Joshua 7). The Plain says "one sinner", as the Hebrew is pointed, and lets the verse lead straight on to 10:1.

a: Dead flies turn a perfumer's oil foul and frothy
p: The Hebrew says 'flies of death', with a singular verb. Most read 'dead flies'; some 'deadly flies'.
b: The Hebrew zevuve mavet is literally "flies of death". This may mean dead flies, or flies that bring death, or it may be a slip for zevuv mavet, "a dead fly", which would match the singular verbs that follow, yav'ish yabbia', "makes stink, makes ferment". The Greek reads "dying flies". The picture is clear either way: a perfumer's costly oil, ruined by a few insects. The English idiom "a fly in the ointment" comes from this verse in the King James Version. Some readers link the flies to Baal-zebub, "lord of flies" (2 Kings 1:2), but nothing in the verse points to him.
orig: זְבוּבֵי מָוֶת יַבְאִישׁ יַבִּיעַ (zevuve mavet yav'ish yabbia')

a: weighs more
p: Yaqar means 'heavy' or 'precious'. A small amount of folly can outweigh a lifetime's wisdom and good name.
b: Yaqar means weighty, precious or costly, and kavod, "honor", comes from the root for "heavy". So the saying weighs things: a little folly is "heavier" than wisdom and honor. One foolish act can undo a good reputation, as one sinner can destroy much good (9:18). The Greek turned the sense around, so that "a little wisdom is more precious than the glory of great folly" (see the variant). The Hebrew is harder and more like Qohelet: wisdom is strong but fragile.
orig: יָקָר מֵחָכְמָה מִכָּבוֹד סִכְלוּת מְעָט (yaqar mechokhmah mikkavod sikhlut me'at)

a: The wise man's heart goes toward his right hand
p: The right hand stood for strength, skill and favor; the left for weakness and bad luck. It has nothing to do with modern politics.
b: In the Bible and throughout the ancient world the right hand is the hand of strength, skill and honor (Exodus 15:6; Psalm 16:8; Psalm 110:1), and the left the weaker or unlucky side; the Latin word for left, sinister, gave English its word for something threatening. In Jesus' parable the sheep stand at the king's right and the goats at his left (Matthew 25:33). So the wise person's heart, his mind and will, leads him the right way, and the fool's leads him wrong. The modern sense of political "right" and "left" began in the French National Assembly of 1789 and has no link to this verse.

a: he is senseless
p: The Hebrew 'his heart is lacking' is Proverbs' phrase for the senseless person.
b: Libbo chaser, "his heart is lacking", is close to Proverbs' chasar lev, "lacking heart", which the site renders "senseless" (Proverbs 6:32; Proverbs 7:7; Proverbs 9:4). The heart is the seat of judgment, so the fool has no good sense. He cannot hide it: even walking down the road he gives himself away. The end of the verse is ambiguous (see the next note).

a: and he tells everyone he is a fool.
p: The Hebrew can mean the fool shows everyone that he is a fool, or that he calls everyone else a fool.
b: The Hebrew is ve'amar lakkol sakhal hu': "and he says to all, he (is) a fool." Most take it to mean that the fool tells on himself: the way he behaves announces his own folly to everyone (so Rashi, Ibn Ezra and most modern versions). The Plain follows this reading. Others read it as the fool's own verdict on others: he thinks everyone he meets is a fool (so the Vulgate and some medieval readers). The Greek has "all that he thinks is folly". The Hebrew allows both, because the bare "he (is) a fool" does not say who is meant.
orig: וְאָמַר לַכֹּל סָכָל הוּא (ve'amar lakkol sakhal hu')

a: If the ruler's spirit rises up against you
p: Ruach here is temper or anger. The advice is to stay put and stay calm, with a play on the word 'rest'.
b: Ruach, wind or spirit, here means the ruler's temper (compare Judges 8:3; Proverbs 16:32). The advice, "do not let go of your place", is for a courtier or official: do not walk out in protest or panic (compare 8:3). The reason has a wordplay, which the Plain carries with one English verb. "Do not let go" is al-tannach and "lets ... go" is yanniach, both from nuach, "rest, leave": do not let go of your place, because calm lets great wrongs go. The second verb can also mean "puts to rest" or "calms". Marpe', "calm", also means healing (Proverbs 14:30; Proverbs 15:4). Proverbs gives the same counsel for dealing with kings (Proverbs 16:14; Proverbs 25:15).
orig: מְקוֹמְךָ אַל־תַּנַּח כִּי מַרְפֵּא יַנִּיחַ (meqomekha al-tannach ki marpe' yanniach)

a: like a mistake that comes out from the one in power
p: Shegagah is the word for an unintended sin in Leviticus. Qohelet may be dry: the ruler's blunder is 'as if' it were innocent.
b: Shegagah is an error made without intent, the term used in the laws on unintended sins (Leviticus 4:2; Numbers 15:22–29). Shallit, "the one in power", is a late word for a ruler or governor (8:8; Genesis 42:6, of Joseph). The little word ke-, "like", may be ironic: the injustice in 10:6–7 is "like" an innocent slip, but it comes from the top, so it does great harm. Others take ke- to mean "truly, indeed" (it is a real error from the ruler). Some hear the caution of an official: in a Persian or Ptolemaic province, "a mistake" was as far as one could safely go in criticizing the government.

a: I have seen slaves up on horses
p: Horses were for the elite. Slaves riding while princes walk was the ancient picture of a society turned on its head.
b: In the ancient Near East, riding a horse was a mark of rank: kings, nobles and royal messengers rode, while ordinary people walked or used donkeys (Esther 6:8–11; Jeremiah 17:25). Persian nobles prided themselves on horsemanship. So the scene in 10:6–7 is the world upside down, a theme found across ancient wisdom: Proverbs speaks of the earth shaking "beneath a slave when he takes the throne" (Proverbs 30:22; compare Proverbs 19:10), and the Egyptian Admonitions of Ipuwer lament that the poor now own riches and the nobles go hungry. Qohelet does not say whether he regrets the old order or simply records that power falls to the wrong people.

a: The one who digs a pit falls into it
p: Proverbs uses this saying of schemers caught in their own trap. Here it may simply describe the risks of ordinary work.
b: The line repeats a well-known saying: "The one who digs a pit falls into it" (Proverbs 26:27; compare Psalm 7:15; Sirach 27:26). There it means that evil comes back on the one who plans it. But 10:8–9 go on to quarrying stones and splitting wood, which are ordinary jobs, not crimes. So many scholars read the four lines as a list of everyday hazards: every task has its risk, and wisdom (10:10) helps one avoid them. Qohelet's word for pit, gummats, is found only here and is related to Aramaic. Amos uses the same picture of the snake: a man leans on a wall at home, and a snake bites him (Amos 5:19).

a: If the iron is blunt
t: A hard verse about an axe
p: This is one of the most difficult verses in the book. The general sense is clear: skill saves effort.
b: Almost every word is debated. Qehah, "blunt", is used of teeth set on edge (Jeremiah 31:29). Lo'-fanim qilqal may mean "has not whetted the face", that is, the cutting edge (the Plain keeps "face"), using a verb that elsewhere means to shake or to polish (Ezekiel 21:21; compare Ezekiel 1:7). Chayalim yegabber, "he increases strength", may mean "he must work harder" or, with a different sense of chayil, "he must bring more soldiers". The last line, veyitron hakhsher chokhmah, puts Qohelet's key word yitron, "gain", beside hakhsher, "to make succeed". The Greek versions differ among themselves (see the variant). The Plain follows the most common reading: with a blunt axe you must strain, but wisdom gives the gain of success.

a: there is no gain for the master of the tongue
p: Snake charming was a known trade. 'Master of the tongue' names the charmer and points ahead to the sayings about speech.
b: Charmers who controlled snakes by whispered spells were known in Israel and Egypt (Psalm 58:4–5; Jeremiah 8:17; Sirach 12:13). Lachash, "whisper, charm", rhymes with nachash, "snake". The charmer is called ba'al hallashon, "master of the tongue", and his skill is worthless if he is too late: a bite before the spell means no fee and possibly no life. The phrase "master of the tongue" also prepares for 10:12–14, which turn from snakes to speech: the wise man's words bring favor, but the fool's tongue destroys him. Later Jewish readers took the master of the tongue as the slanderer, whose words bite like a snake (Bavli Arakhin 15b).

a: Words from a wise mouth are grace
p: Chen is favor or charm. A fool's own lips 'swallow' him, as Proverbs says a fool's mouth wrecks him.
b: Chen means grace in the sense of charm and favor. Wise words win goodwill for the speaker, as in Proverbs 22:11: "whose lips speak grace, / the king is his friend." Paul uses the same idea: let your speech always be with grace (Colossians 4:6). The fool's lips, by contrast, teballe'ennu, "swallow him", the verb used of Sheol and of the earth swallowing Korah (Numbers 16:32; Proverbs 1:12). Proverbs puts it: "His own mouth wrecks the fool" (Proverbs 18:7).
r: Proverbs 22:11; Proverbs 18:7; Proverbs 10:32; Colossians 4:6; Numbers 16:32; Proverbs 1:12

a: Yet the fool piles up words.
t: The fool talks about the future
p: Qohelet's repeated refrain that no one knows the future is set against the fool, who talks on as if he did.
b: Qohelet says again and again that no one can know what will come (3:22; 6:12; 7:14; 8:7; 11:2, 6). Here the refrain is aimed at the fool, who "piles up words" (compare 5:3, 7) as if he had answers. Where the Hebrew has "what is going to happen", the Greek reads "what has been and what will be", as if the first verb were past, and Jerome's Latin also has the past ("what was before him"); see the variant. James gives a Christian form of the same warning: you do not know what tomorrow will bring, so say "if the Lord wills" (James 4:13–15). Jesus' teaching on not fretting over tomorrow draws a calmer conclusion from the same fact (Matthew 6:34).

a: for none of them knows how to get to town
t: Lost on the way to town
p: Probably a saying for someone hopelessly dense. The Hebrew switches from 'fools' to 'him', which the Plain smooths.
b: Literally: "the toil of fools wearies him, who does not know how to go to a city." The switch from plural "fools" to singular "him" is odd; the Plain smooths it with "each of them" in mind. Not knowing the road to town seems to have been a proverb for being too dense to manage the simplest thing, like the English "can't find his way home". Some see a sharper point: the fool tires himself out with work that leads nowhere. The Targum reads it of the fool who does not go to the city of the wise to learn.
orig: אֲשֶׁר לֹא־יָדַע לָלֶכֶת אֶל־עִיר (asher lo'-yada' lalekhet el-'ir)

a: Your king is a lad
p: Na'ar means a boy, but also a servant. Set beside 'a son of free men' in 10:17, it may mean a king of low birth.
b: Na'ar can mean a boy or youth (1 Samuel 17:33), but also a servant or attendant (Genesis 22:3; 2 Kings 5:20). In 10:17 the good king is ben-chorim, "a son of free men". So the contrast may be birth, not age: woe to the land whose king is an upstart servant, like the slave who "takes the throne" in Proverbs 30:22. Most versions take it as age, echoing Isaiah's threat, "I will give them boys for their officials" (Isaiah 3:4). Some scholars who date the book in the third century BC thought of Ptolemy V, who became king of Egypt, and so of Judea, as a small child in 204 BC; most think the saying is general.

a: and your princes eat at daybreak
p: Eating and drinking from the early morning was a sign of leaders who neglect their duties.
b: The main meal came later in the day. Isaiah condemns those who are "up at dawn / chasing after beer" (Isaiah 5:11), and on the day of Pentecost Peter answers the charge of drunkenness by pointing out that it is only nine in the morning (Acts 2:15). The Talmud lists the hours at which different people take their first meal, from gladiators, robbers and idle heirs who eat earliest, to workers, to scholars, who eat last (Bavli Shabbat 10a). Princes who start feasting at daybreak are not judging cases or running the country; 10:17 praises those who eat "at the right time".

a: Happy are you, land!
p: Ashrei, 'happy', is the first word of Psalm 1. 'A son of free men' uses a late word for the nobility.
b: Ashrekh, "happy are you", is the word that opens Psalm 1 (rendered "Happy" throughout the site). The good king is ben-chorim, "a son of free men", from chor, "noble", a word used for the nobles of Jezreel in 1 Kings 21:8 and often for the nobles of Judah in Nehemiah (Nehemiah 2:16; Nehemiah 6:17). The princes eat "for strength" and not bashti, "for drinking", a word found only here and close to Aramaic. The Greek read the letters as "and they will not be ashamed" (see the variant).
orig: אַשְׁרֵיךְ אֶרֶץ שֶׁמַּלְכֵּךְ בֶּן־חוֹרִים ('ashrekh 'erets shemmalkekh ben-chorim)

a: With laziness upon laziness
p: 'Atsaltayim is a dual form, 'two laziness', meaning great laziness. The saying may be about the state as well as the home.
b: Ba'atsaltayim puts the Proverbs word for laziness ('atslah, Proverbs 19:15) in the dual form, "by double laziness", a way of saying "by sheer laziness". Shiflut yadayim, "lowness of hands", pictures hands hanging down, idle. A flat-roofed house of beams and packed earth needed rolling and repair every year, or the rain came through (compare Proverbs 24:30–34 on the lazy man's ruined wall). Set between the sayings on princes (10:16–17, 19–20), the house may also stand for the kingdom: when its rulers feast instead of working, the whole house leaks.

a: and silver answers for it all
p: The verb may mean money 'answers' every need, 'pays for' it all, or 'keeps everyone busy'. Its tone is debated.
b: Hakkesef ya'aneh et-hakkol: "the silver answers the all." 'Anah usually means to answer, so money provides what every need asks for, or pays the bill for the feast and wine. A second verb 'anah, "to be busy with", gives another reading: money keeps everyone occupied (compare 1:13; 5:20). The saying may be the princes' own motto, said with a cynical shrug after 10:16–18, or a plain observation that feasts cost money. It is often quoted as if it praised wealth; in context it may expose the rulers who think silver solves everything. Compare the warning against loving money in 5:10 and 1 Timothy 6:10.

a: for a bird of the sky will carry off the sound
p: Even a whispered curse can reach the king. Persian kings were famous for their network of informers.
b: The Persian kings had officials known as the King's Eyes and the King's Ears. Herodotus shows the office already in his story of the boy Cyrus, who plays at being king and names one playmate the "King's Eye" (Histories 1.114). Xenophon describes how Cyrus rewarded anyone who brought him useful news, so that the king seemed to have many eyes and ears (Cyropaedia 8.2.10–12). Qohelet's readers knew that a careless word could be reported. The bird is a proverbial carrier of secrets, as in the English "a little bird told me"; the Aramaic Words of Ahiqar warn that a word is like a bird, and once released it cannot be caught again. Madda', "thoughts", is a late word for knowledge or mind (2 Chronicles 1:10); the Greek rendered it with syneidesis, the word the New Testament uses for "conscience". Jesus says what is whispered in private rooms will be shouted from the housetops (Luke 12:3).

a: Send your bread out over the surface of the water
t: "Cast your bread": trade, charity or risk?
p: The KJV's 'Cast thy bread upon the waters' has been read as advice on sea trade, on generosity, and on taking risks.
b: Three main readings. Trade: "bread" is grain, and sending it over the water is shipping goods by sea, a venture that pays back only after many days (compare Proverbs 31:14; 1 Kings 10:22). Then 11:2 means spread your cargo over several ships. Charity: give freely, even where you expect nothing back, and the kindness will return. This is the reading of the Targum (give your bread to the poor who sail on ships, and you will find its reward in the world to come), of Rashi, and of most Christian preachers; the Egyptian Instruction of Ankhsheshonq has a close saying: do a good deed and throw it in the river, and when it dries up you will find it. Goethe put a similar Eastern proverb into verse. Risk: the verse is about acting boldly when the outcome cannot be known, which is the theme of 11:1–6. The readings can overlap: Qohelet's point in any case is that waiting for certainty means doing nothing (11:4).
r: 11:2; 11:4; 11:6; Proverbs 31:14; 1 Kings 10:22; Proverbs 19:17; Luke 6:35; Luke 14:12–14; Galatians 6:9

a: Give a share to seven, and even to eight
p: A counting pattern, 'seven, and even eight', means 'as many as you can'. Cheleq, 'share', is Qohelet's word for a portion.
b: The pattern "x, and even x+1" is a way of saying "many, and then some" (Micah 5:5; Proverbs 30:15–31; Amos 1:3). Cheleq, "share" or "portion", is the word Qohelet uses for a person's portion in life (9:6, 9). Here it is something you give away or spread out: either a share of your goods given to many people, which suits the charity reading of 11:1, or your goods divided among many ventures, so that one disaster does not ruin you, which suits the trade reading. The reason given covers both: you do not know what evil is coming. Jewish tradition used the verse for generous giving (Kohelet Rabbah), and Christian teachers for almsgiving to many (compare 1 Timothy 6:18).
orig: תֶּן־חֵלֶק לְשִׁבְעָה וְגַם לִשְׁמוֹנָה (ten-cheleq leshiv'ah vegam lishmonah)

a: the place where the tree falls is where it will be
p: In context, a picture of nature doing what it does whatever we wish. Preachers long read it of a person's state at death.
b: Clouds full of rain will empty, and a fallen tree stays where it falls. Neither can be controlled or reversed by human wishes, so, says 11:4, stop waiting and act. The odd word yehu', "it will be", is found only here. Many Christian preachers, from the Middle Ages on, read the tree as a human being at death: as a person "falls", toward the south (good) or the north (evil), so he remains forever. The reading was used to urge repentance, and by some Protestant writers against purgatory. Most modern interpreters think this goes beyond the verse, which is about the limits of human control in this life.

a: Whoever keeps an eye on the wind will not sow
p: A farmer who waits for perfect weather never plants. Proverbs has the lazy one who will not plow in winter.
b: Sowing needed a still day, so the wind would not scatter the seed, and reaping a dry one. But a farmer who keeps watching the sky for the perfect day will never start. Proverbs makes a similar point about the lazy one: "The lazy one does not plow when winter comes" (Proverbs 20:4). Qohelet's twist is that the problem is not laziness but the wish to be sure first. Ruach here is plainly the wind, which leads into the double sense in 11:5.

a: which way the wind goes
p: Ruach can be wind or the breath of life. The verse may set the wind beside the womb, or picture breath entering a child in the womb.
b: Ruach means wind, breath or spirit. After 11:4 it most naturally means the wind: no one can track its path. The Leningrad Codex goes on with ka'atsamim, "like the bones", in the womb: you cannot know the wind's way, and the same is true of the bones growing in the womb. The Greek agrees ("like bones"). A number of medieval Hebrew manuscripts read ba'atsamim, "in the bones", and with it many modern versions make one picture: how the breath of life comes into the bones of the unborn (Psalm 139:13–16; Job 10:10–12; Ezekiel 37:5–10). See the variant. The Plain keeps two pictures, wind and womb, with "it is the same with" for the Hebrew "like". Jesus joins the two meanings of the word when he tells Nicodemus, "The wind blows where it wants to", and that it is so with everyone born from the Spirit (John 3:8).

a: the God who makes everything
p: Ma'aseh ha'elohim, 'what God does', is Qohelet's phrase for God's work in the world, which no one can fully grasp.
b: Qohelet uses ma'aseh ha'elohim, "the work of God" or "what God does", for God's activity in the world (3:11; 7:13; 8:17). His point is always the same: people can see that God acts but cannot find out the whole of it from beginning to end (3:11; 8:17). Here he says it in the plainest form, adding that God "makes everything". The phrase is not a denial of God's care. It is a reason for humility, and in 11:6 a reason to act without waiting to understand.

a: Plant your seed at dawn
p: Plainly farming advice: keep working, since you cannot know which effort will succeed. The rabbis applied it to students and children.
b: "Morning" and "evening" may be the two ends of a working day, or of a life. The literal sense is a farmer's: sow early, keep at it, because you cannot tell which sowing will grow. Rabbi Akiva applied it to teaching: when his first students died, he raised new ones, saying that one who had students in youth should have students in old age (Bavli Yevamot 62b). The same passage applies it to marrying and having children late in life. Christian readers linked it to Paul's sayings on sowing and not growing weary in doing good (2 Corinthians 9:6; Galatians 6:9).

a: Light is sweet
p: In Hebrew poetry light means life. To 'see the sun' is to be alive.
b: Light is the gift of life (Job 3:16, 20; Psalm 49:19; Psalm 56:13). Job asks, "Why does he give light to the sufferer" (Job 3:20), and of the stillborn child Qohelet says, "It has never even seen the sun" (6:5). So "seeing the sun" means being alive (7:11). After the gloom of 9:1–10, Qohelet sounds a note of plain gratitude: being alive is sweet. The next verse sets that sweetness beside the long darkness that follows.

a: the days of darkness
p: Probably death and the dark of Sheol, which will last far longer than life. Some read it as old age.
b: Most take "the days of darkness" as the time of death, in the dark of Sheol (Job 10:21–22; Psalm 88:12), which will be "many" compared with the years of life. Others take it as the hard days of old age, which 12:1–7 describes. Either way, remembering them is meant to make the reader enjoy the light now, not to spoil it. The closing line, "All that comes is vapor", may mean everything still to come, or every person who comes into the world (compare 1:4; 5:15–16). On "vapor", see 9:9.

a: Walk on
t: A command the rabbis worried about
p: The Torah says not to follow your heart and eyes (Numbers 15:39). The sages almost withdrew the book over this verse.
b: The Torah tells Israel: "You will not go scouting after your own heart and your own eyes" (Numbers 15:39). Qohelet seems to say the opposite. Leviticus Rabbah 28:1 says the sages wanted to withdraw the book because of this line, until they read on: "But know this: for all of it God will bring you into judgment." Then they said, Solomon spoke well. Codex Vaticanus, the great fourth-century Greek manuscript, softens the line itself: "walk in blameless ways, and not in the sight of your eyes" (see the variant). The Jerusalem Talmud draws a different lesson from Qohelet's joy: a person will have to give an account for every good thing he saw and did not enjoy (Yerushalmi Kiddushin 4:12).

a: for all of it God will bring you into judgment
p: Is the judgment in this life or after it? And is the line Qohelet's, or a later editor's?
b: Two questions. When? Qohelet doubts that justice is seen in this life (8:14; 9:2), yet says God will judge (3:17; 8:12–13). Jewish and Christian tradition read 11:9 and 12:14 as the final judgment (so the Targum, and the New Testament's teaching in 2 Corinthians 5:10). Some scholars think Qohelet meant only that God holds people to account in this life, in ways no one can predict. Whose words? A number of nineteenth- and early twentieth-century critics, such as Siegfried, thought this half verse (with 12:1a and 12:13–14) was added by a pious editor to tame the book. Most recent commentators (Whybray, Fox, Seow) think it is Qohelet's own: the call to enjoy life is itself something God will ask about. Joy is a gift to be received and accounted for, not a license.

a: black hair
t: Black hair, or the dawn of life?
p: Shacharut comes either from 'black', the dark hair of youth, or from 'dawn', the morning of life.
b: Shacharut appears only here. It may come from shachor, "black", the dark hair of youth before it turns gray (compare the white blossoms of the almond in 12:5), or from shachar, "dawn", the morning of life. Medieval Jewish commentators were divided between the two. The Greek translated anoia, "folly", and the Syriac "not knowing", perhaps guessing from a different root (see the variant). The first half of the verse tells the young man to put away ka'as, "frustration" (as at 1:18 and 2:23; at 7:3 it is rendered "grief"), and ra'ah, from his flesh. Elsewhere the Plain renders ra'ah "evil" (11:2; 12:1), but here it is harm to the body, so "trouble". Youth is "vapor" here in the sense of brief, not worthless: that is why it should be enjoyed.

a: Remember your Creator
t: Your Creator, your well, your grave
p: The Hebrew form of 'your Creator' is unusual, and readers ancient and modern have heard other words in it.
b: Bor'ekha, "your Creator", is written in a plural form, like 'osay, "my Maker", in Job 35:10 and Isaiah 54:5. Most explain it as a plural of majesty, and every ancient version reads "Creator". But the word sounds like others. Some modern scholars propose be'erkha, "your well", meaning your wife (Proverbs 5:15–18), which would join 9:9; others borkha, "your pit", the grave. The rabbis heard all three at once. Akavya ben Mahalalel taught: know where you came from, where you are going, and before whom you will give account (Mishnah Avot 3:1), and the midrash ties his three words to this verse: your source (be'erkha), your grave (borkha) and your Creator (bor'akha) (Leviticus Rabbah 18:1; Kohelet Rabbah 12:1).

a: in the days of your prime
p: Bechurot is the time of a young man's full strength, the age of the bachur, the 'young man' of 11:9.
b: Bechurot comes from bachur, "young man", the word of address in 11:9: a man in his prime, of age to marry and to fight (Isaiah 62:5; Jeremiah 51:22). The Plain uses "prime" for it in both places (11:9; 12:1). The other word for youth, yaldut, from yeled, "child", is the earlier, boyish stage: "while you are young" in 11:9 and "boyhood" in 11:10. The "days of evil" that follow are the opposite season, old age and its troubles, when a person says "There is no delight for me in them". Barzillai says much the same at eighty, when he can no longer taste food or hear singers (2 Samuel 19:35).

a: before the sun goes dark
p: The poem has been read as an allegory of the aging body, a winter storm, a dying household, and the end of the world.
b: The images in 12:2–7 have been read in four main ways, and many readers combine them. The aging body: each image is a part of the body: the guards are the arms, the men of strength the legs, the grinders the teeth, the women at the windows the eyes, the almond blossom white hair. This is the reading of the Targum, the Talmud (Bavli Shabbat 151b–152a), Leviticus Rabbah 18:1 and Jerome, and it is still the most popular. A storm: the darkening sun and returning clouds are the winter rains, a picture of the gloom of old age (a reading of several nineteenth-century commentators). A house and a funeral: the scene is a great estate falling into ruin (Sawyer), or a household and town in mourning at a death, with servants trembling, mills stopped and mourners in the street (Fox). The end of the world: the darkening of sun, moon and stars is the language of the prophets' day of the LORD (Isaiah 13:10; Joel 2:10), so a person's death is pictured as a small end of the world (Seow, Fox). See the chapter page.

a: and the clouds come back after the rain
p: In Israel's winter, rain comes in bouts with clouds between. In old age, troubles come one after another without clearing.
b: In the land of Israel the rains fall from about October to April, and in midwinter storm follows storm. Clouds returning "after the rain" mean the sky never clears. In old age, readers say, one sorrow follows another without the relief of sunshine between (so the Targum and Rashi, who make the rain a picture of trouble). The verse also echoes the prophets' darkened sky (see the previous note).

a: on the day that the guards of the house shake
p: Guards, strong men, women grinding grain, women at the windows: read as a house, or as a body.
b: Read as a house, this is a large household on a day of disaster: the men who guard it tremble, the strong men stoop, the maids who grind the daily flour (Exodus 11:5; Matthew 24:41) stop work, and the women who watch the street from the lattice windows (Judges 5:28; 2 Samuel 6:16) see only darkness. Read as a body, the guards are the hands and arms, which shake; the strong men are the legs, which bend; the grinders are the teeth, "because they are few"; and the watchers at the windows are the eyes, which grow dim. The two readings fit well together, since the Bible often pictures the body as a house (Job 4:19; 2 Corinthians 5:1).
r: Exodus 11:5; Matthew 24:41; Judges 5:28; 2 Samuel 6:16; Job 4:19; 2 Corinthians 5:1

a: and one wakes up at a bird's call
p: The old wake at the first chirp of dawn, or the voice grows thin as a bird's. 'Daughters of song' may be singers or notes.
b: Veyaqum leqol hatsippor is usually taken as "one rises at the sound of the bird": the old sleep lightly and are up at first light. Others read "the bird rises to sing", nature carrying on while the house goes silent, or "the voice rises to a bird's", the thin voice of age. "The daughters of song" are singers (2 Samuel 19:35, where old Barzillai doubts that he can still hear the singers, men and women), or musical notes, or songbirds. Yishachu, "sink down", pairs with the low sound of the mill: the world grows quiet for one who is going deaf. The "double doors onto the street" may be the ears or lips in the body reading, or simply a house closing for mourning.

a: the almond tree is in bloom
p: The almond flowers white in late winter, before any other tree. Most readers see the white hair of age.
b: The almond is the first tree to blossom in the land, in January or February, and its blossom is white or pale pink. Most readers since Jerome and the rabbis have seen the white hair of old age. The Hebrew verb is pointed yane'ts, which looks as if it came from na'ats, "to spurn" (hence older renderings such as "the almond is despised"), but most take it as a spelling of yanets, "blossoms", as all the ancient versions do. Jeremiah's vision plays on shaqed, "almond", and shoqed, "watching" (Jeremiah 1:11–12). In the house reading, the almond simply blooms while the household mourns: nature goes on as people die.

a: and the caper berry fails
p: Two hard images. The locust 'drags itself' or 'grows fat'; the caper berry, a spur to appetite, 'fails'. The KJV read 'desire'.
b: Yistabbel hechagav means "the locust loads itself" or "becomes a burden". The Greek reads "the locust grows fat". Readers have seen a stiff, heavy gait, the hips of the old, or a swarm of locusts lumbering in spring. Ha'aviyonah appears only here; the Greek, Latin and later Jewish tradition took it as the caper, whose buds were eaten to stir appetite and, it was said, desire. The verb tafer means "break" or "fail" (or "burst open"). The KJV's "desire shall fail" follows the rabbinic reading that the word itself means desire (Bavli Shabbat 152a). Either way, the senses fade: food and love no longer stir.
orig: וְיִסְתַּבֵּל הֶחָגָב וְתָפֵר הָאֲבִיּוֹנָה (veyistabbel hechagav vetafer ha'aviyonah)

a: his house of forever
p: 'House of eternity' was a common name for the tomb in Egypt and among the Phoenicians. It does not here mean heaven.
b: Bet 'olamo, "his house of forever", was a standard way to speak of a grave. Egyptian texts call the tomb a "house of eternity", and Phoenician, Punic and Palmyrene inscriptions use the same phrase as Qohelet for a burial place. Tobit prays to be released "to the everlasting place" (Tobit 3:6), and the Targum here has "his grave". So the meaning is not heaven but the tomb, from which no one returns (compare Job 7:9–10; Job 10:21). Paul turns the phrase around: when the tent we live in on earth is taken down, God has a dwelling for us, not handmade, lasting forever in the heavens (2 Corinthians 5:1).

a: and the mourners circle about in the street
p: Professional mourners, often women, walked the streets wailing at a death.
b: Funerals in Israel were loud and public. Families hired mourners, often women skilled in laments, who wailed in the street and the market (Jeremiah 9:17–18; Amos 5:16; 2 Chronicles 35:25), and flute players joined them (Matthew 9:23). The Mishnah says even a poor man should hire at least two flutes and one wailing woman for his wife's funeral (Mishnah Ketubot 4:4). The "circling" may be a ritual procession. In Qohelet's picture the mourners are already gathering, or are going about their business, while the dying person goes to his house of forever.

a: the bowl of gold
p: Two pictures of a broken life: a golden lamp bowl hanging from a silver cord, and a jar and pulley at a well.
b: The first two images may be one: a golden bowl, the oil reservoir of a lamp (the same word, gullah, is used for the lampstand's bowl in Zechariah 4:2–3), hanging from a silver cord. When the cord is torn, the bowl falls and the light goes out; Proverbs says "The human breath is the LORD's lamp" (Proverbs 20:27). The second pair is a well: the jar breaks at the spring, the wheel or pulley that lowers it is crushed into the cistern. Water and light are both pictures of life (Psalm 36:9; Jeremiah 2:13). The precious materials say that life is costly as well as fragile. Rabbinic and later readers took the silver cord as the spine and the golden bowl as the skull.

a: and the wheel is crushed at the cistern
t: Claude's theory: from Creator to cistern
p: Claude's theory: the poem is framed by a sound play, bor'ekha 'your Creator' (12:1) and habbor 'the cistern' (12:6).
b: This is my own suggestion, not an established reading. The poem begins "Remember bor'ekha", "your Creator" (12:1), and its last picture of breaking ends with the wheel falling "to habbor", "the cistern" or "the pit" (12:6). The two words share the consonants b-r. If the sound play is deliberate, the poem moves from the one who made you to the pit that receives you, and 12:7 then resolves both: the dust goes to the earth and the spirit to God. This overlaps with published work: the emendation borkha, "your pit", in 12:1 (see the note there) and the midrash's triple pun in Leviticus Rabbah 18:1 already link the words. What I add is only that the link may frame the whole poem.

a: and the spirit goes back to God, who gave it
p: Qohelet echoes Genesis: dust to dust, breath to God. Readers divide over whether 'spirit' here is life-breath or a conscious soul.
b: The verse echoes the creation story, where God shapes the man "from dust of the ground" and blows into him "the breath of life" (Genesis 2:7), and the curse, "to dust you will go back" (Genesis 3:19). Psalm 104 says the same: "You gather back their breath, and they die / and go back to their dust" (Psalm 104:29; compare Job 34:14–15). Earlier Qohelet asked, "Who knows whether the spirit of human beings goes up above" (3:21). Now he says that it returns to God. Many scholars think ruach here is the life-breath God lends, which simply goes back to its giver; others read a soul returning to God. Whether the verse teaches a conscious life after death is the question of the card on chapter 3 (see Ecclesiastes 3), which sets the Catholic, Orthodox, Protestant, Adventist and Jehovah's Witness answers side by side. The Talmud draws a moral: give it back to him as he gave it to you, pure (Bavli Shabbat 152b). Jesus and Stephen die commending their spirits to God (Luke 23:46; Acts 7:59).
r: Genesis 2:7; Genesis 3:19; Psalm 104:29–30; Job 34:14–15; 3:19–21; Luke 23:46; Acts 7:59; Psalm 31:5

a: says Qohelet
p: Here the Hebrew has 'the Qohelet', with the article, as if it were a title. The book's motto returns to close Qohelet's words.
b: The motto of 1:2 comes back to close Qohelet's words, framing everything between. Here the Hebrew reads haqqohelet, "the Qohelet", with the article, as if the name were a title or office, "the Gatherer" (see 1:1). Many scholars read 7:27 the same way by dividing its letters differently. Like 1:2, this line is spoken about Qohelet in the third person, "says Qohelet": it is the voice of the frame narrator, who now steps forward in 12:9–14 to speak about Qohelet. On "vapor", see 9:9.

a: Beyond this: Qohelet was wise
p: 12:9–14 speak about Qohelet in the third person. One editor, two editors, or the author himself stepping out of character?
b: Here a new voice speaks about Qohelet, as in 1:1–2 and 7:27. Three views. One frame narrator: the author created Qohelet as a character and speaks in his own voice at the start and end, praising him and placing his words within the fear of God (Fox; compare the frame of Job). Two epilogists: 12:9–11 come from an admiring student or editor, and 12:12–14 from a later, more cautious hand who wanted to make the book safe for use alongside the Torah (a common critical view, held in different forms by Crenshaw and others). A canon-conscious editor: Sheppard argued that 12:13–14 read Qohelet together with the Torah, as Sirach does with wisdom, and so mark the book's place in Scripture. Traditional Jewish and Christian readers took the whole as Solomon's own conclusion. See the chapter page.

a: He weighed, he searched, he put many proverbs in order
p: Three verbs describe a scholar's craft. The last is the verb Qohelet used for 'straightening' what God made crooked.
b: 'Izzen, found only here, probably means "weighed" (from mo'znayim, "scales"); the Greek and the Syriac connected it with 'ozen, "ear", and read "listened" (see the variant). Chiqqer is "searched out". Tiqqen is "made straight" or "set in order", the very verb of 1:15 and 7:13, where Qohelet said no one can straighten what God has made crooked. Commentators note the irony: the man who said life cannot be straightened spent his life straightening proverbs. The picture is of a teacher who tested, studied and arranged sayings, as Solomon was remembered for "Three thousand proverbs" (1 Kings 4:32).

a: words that delight
t: Words of delight, words of truth
p: Qohelet aimed at words that please and words that are true, a pairing Proverbs also values.
b: Divre-chefets, "words of delight", uses the same chefets as "no delight" in 12:1: Qohelet sought words that give pleasure, well-turned and apt (Proverbs 15:23; Proverbs 25:11). Yosher, "uprightness", and divre emet, "words of truth", say they were also honest (Proverbs 22:21). The epilogist thus defends Qohelet against the charge that his sayings were only clever or only bleak. The phrase gave its name to Schoors' study of Qohelet's Hebrew, The Preacher Sought to Find Pleasing Words.
orig: דִּבְרֵי־חֵפֶץ ... יֹשֶׁר דִּבְרֵי אֱמֶת (divre-chefets ... yosher divre 'emet)

a: like ox goads
p: A goad was a pointed stick for driving oxen. Wise words prod and then stick, like nails driven deep.
b: A dorvan was a long stick with a metal point used to drive oxen at the plow; the Philistines charged Israel for "setting the point of an ox goad" (1 Samuel 13:21). The risen Jesus tells Paul that kicking back against the goads only hurts him (Acts 26:14), using a Greek proverb. Wise sayings prick the hearer into motion. The second picture is of masmerot, nails or pegs "driven deep", which hold fast (Isaiah 22:23; Jeremiah 10:4). So wise words both prod and stay put: they disturb, and they last. The Talmud makes the goad the Torah, which steers a person to life, and adds that words of Torah, like a nail, are firm yet grow like a plant (Bavli Hagigah 3b).

a: the masters of collections
p: Ba'ale asuppot may mean collectors of sayings, the collected sayings themselves, or members of the assemblies of the wise.
b: Ba'ale asuppot is literally "masters (or owners) of gatherings". Three readings: the scholars who collect sayings; the collections themselves, "masters" meaning "those characterized by"; or members of assemblies, as in the KJV's "masters of assemblies". The Talmud takes the last: these are the students of the wise who sit in groups and study, some ruling one way and some another, yet all their words "were given by one shepherd" (Bavli Hagigah 3b). The word asuppah, "gathering", is related to Qohelet's own name if that name means "the one who gathers" (see 1:1).

a: They were given by a single shepherd
p: Most readers see God as the shepherd who gives wisdom. Some think of Solomon, Moses or the head of a school.
b: A shepherd carried a goad, so the image follows naturally. Most Jewish and Christian readers take the "one shepherd" as God, the Shepherd of Israel (Psalm 23:1; Psalm 80:1), who is the source of all true wisdom (Proverbs 2:6). The Talmud says: one God gave them, one leader spoke them (Bavli Hagigah 3b), meaning Moses. Some scholars think the shepherd is a human teacher, Solomon or the head of the school whose sayings were collected, and that "one" means simply "a". Christian readers have also heard Jesus' words, "I am the good shepherd" (John 10:11). The capital letter in some English versions reflects the first reading.

a: And beyond these, my son, take warning
p: The rabbis read this as a warning against books outside Scripture, and against neglecting the words of the sages.
b: "My son" is the teacher's address to his student, as throughout Proverbs (Proverbs 1:8, 10), and the only time the epilogue addresses the reader. Veyoter mehemmah, "and more than these", may mean "be warned about anything beyond these" (the words of the wise just praised), or "in addition to these, be warned". The rabbis heard a play on mehumah, "confusion": whoever brings into his house more books than the twenty-four of Scripture brings confusion (Kohelet Rabbah 12:12; compare Yerushalmi Sanhedrin 10:1). The Babylonian Talmud read it the other way round, as a call to take the words of the scribes even more seriously than the Torah's own words (Bavli Eruvin 21b).

a: much study wears out the flesh
p: Lahag, 'study', is found only here. The line is a teacher's half-humorous sigh, much quoted by students.
b: Lahag occurs nowhere else in the Bible; it is usually linked to an Arabic word meaning to be devoted to something, and the ancient versions all understood "study" or "meditation" (Jerome: frequens meditatio). "Making many books has no end" may be a complaint about a flood of writing in the scribe's own day, or simply a warning that study never finishes. The flesh, the body, wears out first. John's Gospel ends with a similar thought: "If they were written down one by one, I do not think the world itself would have space for the books it would take" (John 21:25).
orig: וְלַהַג הַרְבֵּה יְגִעַת בָּשָׂר (velahag harbeh yegi'at basar)

a: The last word, now that everything has been heard
p: In synagogue reading and many printed Hebrew Bibles, verse 13 is read again after verse 14, so the book does not end on 'evil'.
b: Sof davar, "the end of the matter", is a scribe's closing formula (compare Daniel 7:28). Jewish custom does not like a public reading of Scripture to end on a harsh word. So in four books whose last verse ends badly, Isaiah, the Twelve Prophets (Malachi), Lamentations and Ecclesiastes, the verse before the last is repeated after it, and many printed Hebrew Bibles show it again in smaller type. Here that means the reader ends on "Fear God and keep his commands" rather than "good or evil". The rabbis also said the book was kept in Scripture because "its beginning is words of Torah and its end is words of Torah", meaning this verse (Bavli Shabbat 30b).

a: Fear God and keep his commands
t: Fear God and keep his commands
p: Qohelet himself had urged the fear of God (5:7; 7:18; 8:12). The epilogue joins it to the commandments, the language of Deuteronomy.
b: "Fear God" is not new in the book: Qohelet said God acts "so that people will fear him" (3:14) and told his readers to fear God (5:7; 7:18; 8:12–13). What is new is "keep his commands", mitsvotav shemor, the language of Deuteronomy: Moses asks Israel "to fear the LORD your God, to walk in all his ways" and to keep his commands (Deuteronomy 10:12–13). Proverbs and Job put the fear of the LORD at the root of wisdom (Proverbs 1:7; Job 28:28). So the epilogue ties Qohelet's wisdom to Israel's Torah, as Ben Sira later did (Sirach 1:26–27). Some read this as a correction of Qohelet; others as a fair summary of what he had said all along.
r: 3:14; 5:7; 7:18; 8:12–13; Deuteronomy 10:12–13; Deuteronomy 6:2; Proverbs 1:7; Job 28:28; Sirach 1:26–27; Micah 6:8

a: because this is the whole of being human
p: The Hebrew says only 'this is all the human'. The KJV's 'whole duty' adds a word; others read 'this is for every person'.
b: Ki-zeh kol-ha'adam is literally "for this is all the human" or "every human". The KJV, followed by many, added "duty" in italics: "the whole duty of man". Other readings: "this is what every person is about", "this applies to everyone", or "this is the whole of a person": to fear God is what makes a human being whole. Rabbi Elazar said: the whole world was created only for the one who fears God (Bavli Berakhot 6b). Augustine read it as "for this is every man": whoever is not a keeper of God's commands is, in a sense, nothing (City of God 20.3). The Plain keeps the bare Hebrew close: "the whole of being human".

a: into the judgment over all that is hidden
p: God's judgment reaches even what no one saw. The New Testament says the same of the last judgment.
b: Ne'lam is what is hidden, out of sight (Leviticus 4:13; Psalm 90:8). The verse repeats 11:9, "God will bring you into judgment", and widens it to everything done and everything hidden, good or evil. The Greek has "everything overlooked". The New Testament uses the same idea for the last day: God "judges what people keep secret" (Romans 2:16), and the Lord will light up the hidden things of the darkness (1 Corinthians 4:5; compare 2 Corinthians 5:10). The Talmud applies "all that is hidden" even to small acts that disgust or shame another person (Bavli Hagigah 5a). In synagogue reading, 12:13 is read again after this verse (see the note there).
r: 11:9; 3:17; Psalm 90:8; Romans 2:16; 1 Corinthians 4:5; 2 Corinthians 5:10; Matthew 10:26; Revelation 20:12
